extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 19th-century American literary biography and criticism; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Biographical and critical essays on notable 19th-century American writers and reformers, assessing literary style, public influence, moral character, and lecturing. The page collects critical observations and evaluative principles about authors (e.g., Emerson, Alcott) useful for judging literary work and public intellectuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / self-reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The new literature must show self-reliance and an original relation to the universe rather than reliance on tradition: 'Why should not we have a poetry and philosophy of insight and not of tradition?... Build, therefore, your own world!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewed as 'the first great need in a new literature.' The author uses Emerson's 'Nature' and the 'Dial' as exemplars: authors should repudiate stifling conventions, seek original insight, and cultivate an independent voice even at risk of excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation and density of meaning in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Power in writing is measured by the ability to put 'more meaning into words' — to condense thought into compact, potent phrases: 'words are rammed with thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson is praised for matching Tacitus and for translating a laconic Roman phrase more powerfully; the ideal is to compress large meaning into brief, forceful language (e.g., 'They glared through their absences').

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence / capacity to shape public thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's significance includes his ability to stimulate and educate public opinion and literary taste, locally and abroad: 'his influence as a stimulus was quite unequaled' and he 'educated the public mind to himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure includes international reception (e.g., Emerson's influence in England and on thinkers like Carlyle, Tyndall, Matthew Arnold), the role in founding movements (Transcendentalism, 'Dial'), and long-term cultural impact beyond immediate literary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of public speech / lecturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Public delivery — sonorous oratory, studied pauses, and manner — can amplify written thought; a lecturer's manner can make ideas seem off-hand yet weighty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson's thirty- to forty-season lecturing career is cited: delivery traits (pauses, gazes, apparent hesitation preparing a witticism) are part of effective dissemination. Evaluate both content and oratorical technique when judging a public intellectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision, polish, and balance between boldness and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic revision to remove crude or affected passages improves work; preserve vigor while avoiding tame or crude faults (e.g., replacing 'Fine humble-bee!' with 'Burly, dozing humble-bee').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author values boldness over tame 'French correctness' but also shows Emerson's willingness to revise poems to soften rough rhymes and affectations; assess willingness to revise and tasteful balancing of vigor and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of native/local material and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on immediate, local natural and social material ('the woods and waters around him') is praised as authentic and a source for a distinct national literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson's use of local allusion is seen as an artistic strength that helped create an American literature; value work that uses familiar/local subject matter with imaginative seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral courage and public engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in reform and taking public moral stances (e.g., anti-slavery preaching, supporting woman suffrage) are part of an author's public worth: Emerson 'twice opened his pulpit for anti-slavery addresses' and signed suffrage calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors may consider moral consistency and courage in controversial causes as part of the subject's character and public significance, not merely textual merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic coherence versus aphoristic/fragmentary thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may be judged either by coherent systematic philosophy or by the power of aphoristic, fragmentary insight; lack of systematic statement is not necessarily a defect ('Emerson never desired to ... form a creed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between system-makers and aphorists: evaluate whether the work's fragmentary, condensed form is a deliberate strength (epigrammatic insight) or a weakness (lack of development), using the author's aims and historical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical taste and partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic's judgments reflect personal taste and may be whimsical or partial (e.g., Emerson's fluctuating views of Whitman or Shelley); awareness of such partiality matters when evaluating critical pronouncements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Emerson's occasional whimsy in poetry criticism and his recoil from certain writers; treat individual critical judgments as informative about taste and temperament rather than objective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal temperament and dignity of style
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble, calm nature and freedom from petty antagonisms enhance a writer's stature: 'a nature so noble and so calm that he was never misled ... by controversy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors are encouraged to weigh the author's personal bearing — equanimity, civic dignity, and temper — as contributory to their overall literary and public reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and variety of knowledge informing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich, varied learning enriches style ('Emerson's style was enriched by varied knowledge'); limited reading can make prose or lectures less stimulating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare authors on the range of their allusions and learning: breadth tends to produce a more resourceful style; narrow reading may produce charm but also fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to lecturing: conversation versus monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of public address affects reception: Alcott called his talks 'conversations' but could be unhappy if interrupted, while Emerson's gracious lecturing involved the audience in thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public addresses, consider whether the speaker fosters audience engagement and how mode (conversational vs. formal lecture) suits the speaker's aims and temperament.
